title: the plugin owns only the guard rules only it can know
description: Human-written (guard-reading code). Tasks: (1) Measure which share of 3.0.x guard refusals hit generic destructive operations the host would block anyway. (2) Design: keep plan scope, journal/manifest integrity and recorded-SHA protection; ship a recommended permissions.deny fragment for the rest. (3) One release reports instead of blocking the moved rules, then remove them. Risk: users without auto mode get only spelling-based permission rules; SECURITY.md must say so.
desiredOutcome: the plugin's command-reading guards keep the verdicts that depend on the plan and its own state, and generic destructive-command blocking is left to Claude Code's own layers through a recommended permissions fragment, with SECURITY.md saying which layer holds which guarantee

findings.issue: QUICKSTART's install-check step still recommends deny entries Read(.env*) and Grep(.env*) while the new note says to replace them because an appended Read(.env*) after the carve-outs denies .env.example again; the doctor's secret-rules fix text still says to add Read(.env*). The design recorded Grep(.env*) as having no documented effect.
findings.resolution: fixed in P110.5-exo (cf885925): Make the install-check step's snippet the shipped template or a pointer to it so the page recommends one fragment, and have the doctor's fix text name the template, pinned by a case.

findings.issue: Gitignore-style Read(.env) and Read(credentials) also match directories of that name (a .env virtualenv, a credentials package), which the $-anchored guard regex never refuses; Read(*.pem) hits public certificates and CA bundles; and the fragment's sandbox switch makes those denies OS-level for every subprocess and limits writes to the working directory, while sibling phase worktrees live outside it. No document names these costs, and the design calls the path entries SECRET_PATH spelled as gitignore patterns.
findings.resolution: fixed in P110.5-exo (cf885925): Name the costs and the carve-outs a user would add in the QUICKSTART note, and correct the design sentence to say where the gitignore form is broader than the regex, keeping the template byte-identical to the design block.

findings.issue: SECURITY.md states Claude Code's behaviour (auto mode allows dotenv reads; a deny rule matches spelling; no rule can name an MCP payload path) in the present tense with no basis beside it, though it rests on one reading on CLI 2.1.291 that the design says must be re-read before a release relies on it.
findings.resolution: fixed in P110.5-exo (cf885925): Carry the basis inline - the version and date read and a pointer to the design - or tie the sentence to a re-read step.

findings.issue: The doctor's _is_env_read_deny counts a ! carve-out such as Read(!.env.example) as a rule that refuses dotenv reads, so a merged fragment lists the carve-outs as refusing rules and a carve-out-only list would pass.
findings.resolution: fixed in P110.5-exo (cf885925): Reject a !-prefixed argument, with a case for a carve-out-only list proven red first.

findings.issue: The paragraph says the history guard asks whether a git command would orphan a recorded commit; it refuses force-push, force-with-lease, --orphan, filter-branch and rebase whenever any SHA is recorded, and only the reset arm asks about orphaning.
findings.resolution: fixed in P110.5-exo (cf885925): Say it refuses history rewrites in a repository whose manifest records a commit, and for reset whether one would be orphaned.

findings.issue: The measurement's table still files secret reads as plugin-only by construction, which its own text and the design correct.
findings.resolution: fixed in P110.5-exo (cf885925): Say the rule depends on the pattern, not plugin state, pointing at the design's correction.

findings.issue: A wrong author-enforced count ('Two placements' introducing three bullets) and references to a private task or phase a public reader cannot see.
findings.resolution: fixed in P110.5-exo (cf885925): Drop the count and restate each task or phase reference as the question itself.

findings.issue: The template check turns the deny list into a set, so the load-bearing order (carve-outs after Read(.env.*)) is held only by the byte comparison; the Bash entries have no drift check against the guard's env-dump shapes.
findings.resolution: fixed in P110.5-exo (cf885925): Assert each carve-out's index is after Read(.env.*), proven red on a reordered scratch copy.

review.outcome: phase review (audit-reviewer, phase mode, no project skill): findings fixed by one fix task over the fragment, the doctor and the documents [findings: 8 - 0 high, 3 med, 5 low; 8 with a recorded fix commit]

summary: The plugin's guards were measured and designed against Claude Code's own layers, and no rule moved: every guard refusal of the 3.0.x era depended on plan, manifest, recorded-commit or secret-pattern state, and the guards hold no generic-destructive rule to hand over. The secret-read rules stay for coverage, because Claude Code's permission rules are opt-in and auto mode allows reading the agent's own credentials by default (one reading of the docs and auto-mode defaults on CLI 2.1.291, stated as such). A recommended permissions.deny fragment ships as a template beside the guards, kept in step with the secrets guard's own data by a total drift check; QUICKSTART and the doctor point at that one fragment and name its costs; SECURITY.md says which layer holds which guarantee. The task that would have retired rules was cancelled because the design found none to retire. The desired outcome is met as the evidence left it: the guards keep the plan- and state-dependent verdicts, and generic destructive blocking belongs to Claude Code's layers, where the plugin recommends a fragment rather than moving anything.

tasks.title: which share of 3.0.x guard refusals the host would have stopped anyway is measured
tasks.description: docs/research/guard-refusals-by-owner.md classifies every audit-plugin guard refusal in the private redacted miner corpus (quality-gates-internal: reports/2026-10-05-deep-analysis/experiments/classifier-events.redacted.jsonl). It counts the rows with source plugin-hook and an audit-plugin: subsource, dated from the v3.0.0 tag on 2026-09-18; the repo's own .claude/hooks are excluded. Each refusal is classified by what the verdict depended on: plan scope, journal or manifest integrity, a SHA the manifest records, a secret read, or a generic destructive operation. For each generic row it states whether Claude Code's own layers would have stopped it, and on what basis: a documented auto-mode block category, or a permissions.deny rule that matches the command as written. A row with no basis is counted as undetermined and never folded into either side. Command text is redacted, so classification reads the rows' shape and tags fields. The table carries the inline python3 command that re-derives it, with no new .py and no machine path, and the document says that a public reader cannot re-run it against the private corpus. Its answer, the share of refusals that only the plugin could have made, is the input to the design task.

outcome.technical: docs/research/guard-refusals-by-owner.md classifies the audit-plugin guard refusals in the private redacted miner corpus since the v3.0.0 tag by tracing each refusal label to the hook branch that returns it: plan scope, journal or manifest integrity, a recorded SHA, a secret read, or a generic destructive operation. The generic class is empty in this corpus and era, because every deny arm in the two guards is gated on plan, manifest, SHA or secret state, so the host-basis column has nothing to assess, and the document says so with that basis. It carries an inline command that re-derives the table from a CORPUS path the reader supplies, names no machine path or task id, states that a public reader cannot re-run it, attributes the manifest-path label to both hooks that emit it, and states plainly that the guard misreads a literal stash marker in the command as a command (a false positive), which is why that marker is split.
outcome.descriptive: The guard refusals of the 3.0.x era are classified by what each verdict depended on. None of them was a generic destructive-command block that Claude Code's own layers would have made anyway: every one depended on the plan, the manifest, a recorded commit or a secret pattern.

intentCheck.basis: audit-reviewer (task mode): classification supported by the cited hook lines; one medium (task id in prose) and two low findings fixed as proposed; counts re-derived unchanged

tasks.title: a design splits guard rules into those only the plugin can know and a recommended permissions.deny fragment
tasks.description: docs/research/guard-ownership-design.md goes through each rule in guard-secrets-read.py and guard-history-rewrite.py, and the _config readers they use. For each, it states whether the plugin keeps it (plan scope, journal and manifest integrity, protection of SHAs the manifest records) or hands it to Claude Code's own layers, using the refusal measurement as its basis. It gives the exact recommended permissions.deny fragment as JSON. For each moved rule it names the fragment entry that covers it and what that entry misses, because permission rules match a command's spelling, not its operation. It fixes the transition: one release in which the moved rules report instead of blocking, then removal. It names who loses coverage: users without auto mode get spelling-based rules only. It drafts the SECURITY.md paragraph saying which layer holds which guarantee. It checks whether any config key a moved rule reads would stop being read, which COMPATIBILITY.md makes a major release.

outcome.technical: docs/research/guard-ownership-design.md goes rule by rule through guard-history-rewrite.py and guard-secrets-read.py and the _config readers they call, and decides that no rule moves to Claude Code's own layers. The history arms all depend on plan, manifest or recorded-SHA state that only the plugin holds. The secret-read rules hold no plugin state, but they are kept for coverage: the host's permission rules are opt-in, and auto mode's defaults allow an agent to read its own credentials. The document corrects the refusal measurement's reason for placing secret reads (pattern-only, not plugin-only), gives a recommended permissions.deny fragment that errs toward refusing, names who loses coverage, fixes the transition and compatibility rules for any later move (the config keys both guards read, stateDir included), and drafts a SECURITY.md paragraph. The doctor sentences are narrowed to what _doctor_setup._is_env_read_deny actually reads. The host-layer half rests on one reading (docs fetched and `claude auto-mode defaults` read on 2026-10-06, CLI 2.1.291); the reviewer's independent re-check was refused by the auto-mode classifier and is left to the maintainer. Checks run on the file: _deps.doc_prose_numbers over it reported 0, and the fragment block parses as JSON.
outcome.descriptive: A design document decides, rule by rule, which guard rules only the plugin can enforce and which Claude Code's own layers could hold, and concludes that none should move yet.

intentCheck.basis: audit-reviewer (task mode): plugin-state half verified against the guards' code; one medium (doctor claims overstated) and four low findings fixed and spot-checked; the host-layer half rests on one reading because the reviewer's re-check was refused by the auto-mode classifier, which the document states

tasks.title: generic destructive-command rules are retired from the guards: one release reports, the next removes
tasks.description: Implements the design. For one release, the moved rules answer with a recorded report instead of a deny. The fragment ships as plugins/audit/templates/permissions-deny.example.json, with a pointer from QUICKSTART.md. The code is deleted only after that release has shipped, as a follow-up task added at that point, because one task cannot span two releases. The kept rules (plan scope, journal and manifest integrity, recorded-SHA protection) keep their deny cases, each proven red-first. This is guard-reading code. An executor attempts it first, because the maintainer wants code written by agents. The model's safeguard may stop that attempt. If it does, the refusal is recorded verbatim with /audit:task note, the task is blocked and handed to the human maintainer, and nobody rewords the work to get past the stop. Blocked by P108, because P108's verdict table (operation class by tier, asserted over the hook corpus) holds the rows this change moves. The design's SECURITY.md paragraph lands with the release. If P109 has already moved the suite, the test paths are under its new root.

plugins/audit/tests/test_guard_secrets_read.py: each read shape the design moves reports and names the fragment entry that covers it, and every shape the design keeps is still denied

outcome.descriptive: Cancelled: The ownership design (docs/research/guard-ownership-design.md) found no rule to retire: every history arm depends on plan, manifest or recorded-SHA state only the plugin holds, and the secret-read rules are kept for coverage because Claude Code's permission rules are opt-in and auto mode's defaults allow an agent to read its own credentials. The part of the phase outcome that still applies - the recommended fragment and the SECURITY.md paragraph - moves to its own task with no guard code.

tasks.title: the recommended permissions.deny fragment ships beside the guards, and SECURITY.md says which layer holds which guarantee
tasks.description: Ship the fragment from docs/research/guard-ownership-design.md as plugins/audit/templates/permissions-deny.example.json, byte-for-byte the design's JSON block, and point to it from QUICKSTART.md as an optional step for users who want Claude Code's own layer to refuse secret reads too (no guard rule is replaced: the plugin's guards stay as they are). Land the design's draft SECURITY.md paragraph saying which layer holds which guarantee, adjusted to what this release actually ships. Add a case to the secrets guard's suite that the shipped template parses, equals the design's JSON block, and has a Read() entry for every secret-path family the guard's SECRET_PATH and _CRED_EXT name (or names the omission deliberately), so the template cannot drift from the guard silently. The doctor comparison against the fragment is out of scope.

add: plugins/audit/tests/test_guard_secrets_read.py: the shipped permissions-deny template parses, equals the design's JSON block, and covers every secret-path family the secrets guard names (or names the omission)

outcome.technical: plugins/audit/templates/permissions-deny.example.json ships the recommended fragment, byte-identical to the JSON block in docs/research/guard-ownership-design.md (the design needed no correction). QUICKSTART.md gains an optional "Harden it further" note after the numbered first-run steps: the plugin's guards already refuse secret reads by matching tool-call text; Claude Code's permissions.deny rules match text too, and only its sandbox turns a Read deny into an OS-level block; merge the fragment into the same .claude/settings.json, replacing the install-check step's Read(.env*) and Grep(.env*) entries, because a Read(!...) carve-out reaches only rules before it in the same file. SECURITY.md lands the design's "Which layer holds which guarantee" paragraph, naming the shipped template and stating that it replaces no guard rule. PLUGIN-BUILD-GUIDE.md lists the template and says what the new cases check. test_guard_secrets_read.py's gs-template stage (gs-tpl0..gs-tpl21 with 11b/11c) pins the template to the design's block and to the guard's own data: SECRET_PATH's alternation is split at top level (escapes, classes and groups honoured), every alternative is classified by an anchored full match or reported as drift unless named in an explicit omission list, every member of every family must have its own Read() entry, grouped extensions are expanded, the carve-outs must equal exactly the names the guard's negative look-ahead grants, and the pattern may carry no unescaped VERBOSE comment the splitter would misread. Red: the helper proved gs-tpl0 at HEAD (383/384, the template absent); the drift and exact-set cases were proved red on hand-copied, mutated pattern text and a mutated template in a scratch probe (a second id_ alternative, a secrets.env line, a second credentials extension group, a same-line .p7b, a grouped jks|bks, a .netrc line, Read(!.env.*) and Read(!*.pem) each failed its named case); the hook was never edited. Suite 407/407.
outcome.descriptive: Users who want Claude Code itself to refuse secret reads too can merge a shipped settings fragment; the security document now says which layer holds which guarantee, and a test keeps the fragment in step with the plugin's own secret rules.

outcome.technical: One recommendation, its costs named, and its basis carried. _doctor_setup._is_env_read_deny no longer counts a !-prefixed carve-out as a refusing rule, and the secret-rules fix text tells the user to merge plugins/audit/templates/permissions-deny.example.json (PERMISSIONS_TEMPLATE), keeping its order, instead of adding Read(.env*) (cases ds0h2-ds0h6; helper red 88/92 at HEAD). QUICKSTART's install-check step points at the template instead of carrying its own Read(.env*)/Grep(.env*) snippet, and its optional hardening note names the template's costs: Read(.env) and Read(credentials) also match a directory of that name and everything under it (rename a .env virtualenv to .venv), Read(*.pem) matches public certificates and CA bundles (with a carve-out example placed after it), carve-outs come after the rule they carve from, and the sandbox makes the denies OS-level and limits Bash writes while phase worktrees sit beside the repository - the write limit stated with no dated reading behind it and a pointer to Claude Code's /sandbox panel. SECURITY.md's layer paragraph carries one inline basis for every statement about Claude Code's behaviour (the permissions, sandboxing and permission-modes docs and `claude auto-mode defaults`, read on 2.1.291 on 2026-10-06, quoted in the design, to be re-read before a release relies on them), and its history clause says the guard refuses a history rewrite in a repository whose manifest records a commit and, for reset --hard, whether a recorded commit would be orphaned. The design says where the gitignore form is broader than the guard's end-anchored regex, with its JSON block unchanged; the measurement document's secret-read row says the rule depends on a pattern, not plugin state, and both research documents restate references to a private task or phase as the questions themselves. The template check asserts every carve-out comes after Read(.env.*) (gs-tpl22, with fixture cases 22b and 22c showing the reader fires; the shipped template is already ordered, so gs-tpl22 locks the order rather than having been red).
outcome.descriptive: The quick-start, the doctor and the security document now point to the one shipped permissions fragment, say what it costs a project (a .env virtual environment, public certificates, the sandbox's write limit), and say where their claims about Claude Code come from.
